messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo Reyes is a 24-year-old Colombian American QA engineer who presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after surviving a mass transit disaster in which a commuter bus he was riding collided with a fuel tanker at a highway interchange. The crash resulted in multiple fatalities and dozens of injuries. Mateo had been seated near the rear of the vehicle and was able to escape through a broken window, but the passenger beside him — a woman he had briefly spoken with during the ride — did not survive. He had seen her clearly in the moments before impact, had even made eye contact with her when the first jolt hit, and had not been able to reach her in the chaos that followed. He walked away with minor lacerations. She did not walk away at all.

In the weeks after the crash, Mateo returned to his job at a software firm where his work involves systematically identifying failures in complex systems — a professional irony that has not been lost on him. He sits at his desk running test scenarios for hours each day, and when a colleague stops by to describe a fender-bender on their commute or a news alert surfaces on a shared screen about a highway pileup, something shifts in Mateo's body before he can choose otherwise. The sounds, the vocabulary of collision — even the phrase "point of impact" in a software context — are enough to pull the ground slightly out from under him, producing a creeping sense of unreality, as though he is watching himself from a short distance. It is in precisely these moments, when the triggers catch him off guard at work or at home, that his mind moves almost involuntarily toward a particular kind of thinking: what if he had taken the earlier bus, what if he had sat in a different row, what if he had grabbed her arm. He has come to understand, on some level, that this counterfactual rehearsal is his mind's attempt to locate the point of failure — consistent, perhaps, with his professional instincts — but it brings no resolution, only a deepening conviction that he made the wrong choices and that the wrong choices cost someone her life.

That conviction — that he failed to protect a stranger who had done nothing but sit beside him — has settled into something close to a fixed belief. He was certain he should have done more, that a better version of himself would have. This appraisal of personal failure has not remained contained to the crash itself; it has expanded outward into a broader sense that the world is populated by unpredictable harm and that he, specifically, is not equipped to navigate it. He had come to believe that you can never truly know who or what will harm you next, and alongside this ran a quieter but equally corrosive certainty that nothing good was coming for him — that the crash had closed something off permanently, that the life he had been building was no longer available to him. These beliefs, in turn, have shaped his behavior in ways that have become structurally significant. He avoids television almost entirely, having cancelled a streaming subscription he once used daily. He takes deliberate routes to avoid police vehicles, which he associates with the aftermath of the scene. These avoidances feel, to him, like reasonable precautions given what he now knows about the world, but they have progressively narrowed his life.

The counterfactual thinking, which flares most intensely in the wake of triggers, has not produced any sense of mastery or closure. Instead it feeds directly back into his appraisals — each imagined alternative timeline confirming that he failed, that the world is dangerous, that the future is foreclosed — and those appraisals make the next encounter with a news headline or a crash discussion feel more threatening still.

What finally brought Mateo to seek help was a team meeting in which a colleague casually described a near-miss on the freeway. He dissociated so completely that he lost nearly twenty minutes of the meeting and had to ask a coworker to recap what had been decided. He is most afraid, he said during intake, that this is simply who he is now. What he is most hoping for, though he said it quietly, is to find out that it isn't.
